rv.q: Though Santiago-Hudson doesn't pull off a production that keeps that engine consistently blazing, he — as a superb actor of Wilson himself — does make space for us to meet these people in all their fullness. And that's not nothing.
It's a towering achievement of American drama, and in the hands of director Ruben Santiago-Hudson and a magnificent ensemble, it's nothing short of breathtaking.
Seeing this production of Seven Guitars is like getting an intimate look at the conversations that happen between the scenes of a life, and feeling grateful for the privilege.
Santiago-Hudson has taken the reins of Lincoln Center Theater's profoundly moving production of Seven Guitars.
With this Lincoln Center Theater revival, it also helps to have a cast and a director—Ruben Santiago-Hudson, who won a Tony for playing Canewell in 1996—fully in tune with Wilson's idiom.

If such exchanges furnish much of the pleasure of the play, they also elongate it, requiring patience, or at least a willingness to sync with the leisurely pace of the play, which often seems at odds with the urgency built into the plot.
He’s hoping to reconnect with his ex, Vera (Kristolyn Lloyd), who rightly questions his fidelity, as well as his old bandmates, Canewell (Daniel J. Watts) and Red Carter (Michael Potts).
Seven Guitars is a slow burn. But in a backyard intimate enough to reach out and touch, the time spent in Steel City is well worth it.
